texts.title: The language café
texts.text: Every Wednesday evening, a small café in the city centre is a language café. Students from many countries sit together at big tables. Lucas is twenty-five years old, and he is from Brazil. His Portuguese and Spanish are excellent, and his English is quite good now. At his table there is a woman from Japan and two men from Italy. They ask simple questions: Where are you from? What do you do? Lucas is a nurse, and he is happy to answer. At ten o'clock the café closes, but the new friends are not tired. They are only happy to talk.

texts.title: The new neighbour
texts.text: There is a new neighbour in the building. Her name is Amélie, and she is from France. She is not a student; she is a photographer. She doesn't work in an office — she works at home, and she travels a lot. The people in the building are curious, but they are also shy, so they don't talk to her. Then one morning, Ben meets her at the door. "Are you the new neighbour?" he asks. "Yes, I am," she says, "and I am happy to be here." Now they are friends, and she isn't alone in the building.

texts.title: The blue umbrella
texts.text: It is a rainy Monday, and the classroom is full of umbrellas. "Whose umbrella is this?" the teacher asks. It is a big blue umbrella, and it is next to my chair. "It isn't mine," says Marta. "My umbrella is green." "Is it yours, Pedro?" "No, it isn't. My things are in my bag." Then Daniel comes in, wet and tired. He looks at the blue umbrella and laughs. "That's my umbrella! It's my father's umbrella, and he needs it today." The class laughs too. Daniel takes his umbrella, and the teacher writes on the board: your, my, his, her.

texts.title: The night shift
texts.text: Paolo is a baker, and he works at night. His shift starts at eleven o'clock in the evening, and it finishes at seven in the morning. First, he makes the bread; then he makes the cakes. He never works alone — his cousin works with him, and they talk while they work. Paolo usually sleeps from nine in the morning to three in the afternoon. On Sundays he doesn't work, and he has lunch with his family. His neighbours sometimes ask him: "Do you like your job?" "Yes," he says, "the city is quiet, the bread smells wonderful, and my mornings are free."

texts.title: A walk in the new city
texts.text: Nadia is new in town, and today she explores on foot. In her street there is a small supermarket, a bakery and a bookshop — everything is very close, so she doesn't need the bus. She walks to the river and turns left. There, she can see the old bridge and a big park. In the park there are children, dogs and a lot of green space. She can't visit the museum because it is closed on Mondays, but she can sit in the sun. A man with a dog gives her directions to the market: "Go straight, cross the bridge, and the market is on your right." She thanks him and walks on.

texts.title: The language-exchange evening
texts.text: Last Thursday, Ines went to a language exchange at a bar in the old town. She wanted to practise her English, so she sat with a group from Manchester. At first she could only smile and nod. But after half an hour the words started to come. They talked about films, football and the differences between Spanish and English breakfasts. She didn't leave until eleven, and she wrote down fifteen new expressions on the tram home.

texts.title: A small accident
texts.text: While Carlos was cooking dinner on Sunday, he heard a crash from the living room. His cat, Luna, had jumped onto the bookshelf and knocked down his favourite cup.
